title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
text:
# Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment

- Accession: PSI-106
- Acronym: SLICE
- PSI page: https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-106
- DOI: 10.60555/pm12-rg61
- License: CC0-1.0 (Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal)
- Research area: Combustion Science
- Sub-area:
- Project type: Microgravity Investigation
- Flight program: International Space Station (ISS)
- Hardware:
- Start:
- End:
- NASA center: Glenn Research Center (GRC)

## Objectives

Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.

## Approach

The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.

## Hypothesis

The hypothesis is that the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition and are fundamentally different than flames observed on Earth.

## Research impacts

1. Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth.
2. Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions.
3. Insights into flame stability and behavior to enhance fire safety.
4. Findings will inform the development of cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners.

title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
text:
# Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

- Accession: PSI-107
- Acronym: SPICE
- PSI page: https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-107
- DOI: 10.60555/9kbh-e962
- License: CC0-1.0 (Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal)
- Research area: Combustion Science
- Sub-area: Fire Safety
- Project type: Microgravity Investigation
- Flight program: International Space Station (ISS)
- Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
- Start:
- End:
- NASA center: Glenn Research Center (GRC)

## Objectives

The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments.

Specific objectives were:
(1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
(2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points.
(3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures.
(4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions.
(5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.

## Approach

The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.

## Hypothesis

The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames. Flame properties are expected to differ significantly from those observed under normal gravity.

## Research impacts

(1) Will improve our understanding of soot formation mechanisms and help design safer spacecraft environments.
(2) Will contribute to refining our computational models for predicting flame behaviors under non-buoyant conditions.
(3) Will enhance our knowledge of soot generation
(4) Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.

title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity
text:
# Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

- Accession: PSI-115
- Acronym:
- PSI page: https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-115
- DOI: 10.60555/q0v5-1v28
- License: CC0-1.0 (Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal)
- Research area: Combustion Science
- Sub-area: Smoke Aerosol, Combustion Simulation
- Project type: Ground Investigation
- Flight program: Not Applicable
- Hardware:
- Start: 01-30-2017
- End: 12-31-2019
- NASA center: Glenn Research Center (GRC)

## Objectives

The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.

## Approach

The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined. Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source.

## Hypothesis

Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated.

## Research impacts

Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text:
# Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

- Accession: PSI-117
- Acronym:
- PSI page: https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-117
- DOI: 10.60555/gz0q-b577
- License: CC0-1.0 (Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal)
- Research area: Combustion Science
- Sub-area: Droplet
- Project type: Ground Investigation
- Flight program:
- Hardware:
- Start: 02-15-2017
- End: 02-14-2022
- NASA center: Glenn Research Center (GRC)

## Objectives

The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

## Approach

OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.

## Hypothesis

External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.

## Research

title: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
text:
# Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

- Accession: PSI-142
- Acronym:
- PSI page: https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-142
- DOI: 10.60555/80qf-vj95
- License: CC0-1.0 (Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal)
- Research area: Combustion Science
- Sub-area: Spacecraft Fire Safety
- Project type: Ground Investigation
- Flight program: Not Applicable
- Hardware: Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware
- Start: 08-01-2016
- End: 07-31-2021
- NASA center: Glenn Research Center (GRC)

## Objectives

By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
 1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
 2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
 4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
 5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.

## Approach

Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].

## Hypothesis

This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport

text:
[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].

## Hypothesis

This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.

## Research impacts

Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
text:
# Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

- Accession: PSI-159
- Acronym: ACME CFI-G
- PSI page: https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-159
- DOI: 10.60555/cyt1-kh64
- License: CC0-1.0 (Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal)
- Research area: Combustion Science
- Sub-area: Flames of Gaseous Fuels
- Project type: Microgravity Investigation
- Flight program: International Space Station (ISS)
- Hardware: ACME, Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
- Start:
- End:
- NASA center: Glenn Research Center (GRC)

## Objectives

1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.

## Approach

Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.

## Hypothesis

The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

## Research impacts

Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

title: ACME BRE structured summary
text:
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE), NASA PSI investigation PSI-20.
Program: ACME.
Hardware: CIR.
Platform: ISS.
Years: 2010-2025.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. - Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). - Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
Fuel phase: gas.
Fuels: methane, ethylene, propylene, methanol, ethanol, acetone, polyethylene, polymethylmethacrylate, polypropylene, polystyrene.
Sample geometry: porous circular burners.
Diluents: nitrogen, carbon dioxide.
Tested conditions: Oxygen 21 to 34%; Pressure 8.2 to 14.7 psi; Pressure 56.537 to 101.353 kPa.
Variables varied: burner size, oxygen concentration, pressure, fuel flow rate, fuel mixture.
Tests recorded: 18.
Key findings: - BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. - Burning on flat plates was studied at various orientations with respect to gravity. Flat wicks of ceramic (Kaowool PM) board (10 cm wide and 1–10 cm long) were saturated with methanol or ethanol. Steady flames were obtained that ranged from boundary layer flames to plume-type burning. The onset of unsteady flow and transition to turbulence commenced at Grashof numbers of 10 6 –10 7 , increasing with decreasing angle (toward underside burning). - The burning rate emulator (BRE) is a burner that emulates condensed fuel flames using gaseous fuel/inert mixtures by matching four properties: the heat of combustion; the heat of gasification; the laminar smoke point; and the surface temperature. Matching the heat of gasification requires measuring the burner heat flux, for which the BRE has embedded heat flux gauges and a copper top‐plate calorimeter.
Extinction findings: - The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.
Fire safety relevance: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time..

title: BASS-II structured summary
text:
Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II), NASA PSI investigation PSI-25.
Program: BASS-II.
Hardware: MSG.
Platform: ISS, drop_tower.
Years: 2014-2018.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - To identify the worst-case flammability conditions for materials in spacecraft environments and compare them to terrestrial screening tests. - To test the hypothesis that materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation burn as well as or better than in normal gravity under identical conditions. - To examine how thermal and species fields diverge and lead to microgravity flame extinguishment by varying fuel thickness. - Evaluate the flammability of Nomex since it is heavily used aboard the International Space Station as a fire barrier - Burn any unused Burning and Suppression Solids - I (BASS-I) samples, of which there was a single wax candle - Further understand the mechanisms controlling the spread of flames over the surface of solid combustible materials, particularly in a spacecraft environment - Determine the effects of microgravity on the spread of flames over polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) rods of different diameters subjected to different O2 concentrations and low flow velocities - Study flame growth, spread, and extinction over a composite cotton-fiberglass fabric blend in low-speed concurrent forced flows - Determine the low-speed quenching flammability boundary of materials as a function of oxygen percentage - Examine the role of radiation- and solid-phase conductive losses on the flame - Study spacecraft materials flammability evaluation test methods - Estimate the temperature rise of the BASS experiment assembly for a worst-case flame for a large thick sample - Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. - Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. - Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements. - Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections.
Fuel phase: solid.
Fuels: polymethylmethacrylate, cotton-fiberglass blended fabric, cellulose, Nomex, wax, PMMA, cotton-fiberglass fabric, Japan Wax, SIBAL, composite fabric, paraffin, Nomex III, SIBAL fabric, candle.
Sample geometry: rods, slabs, spheres, and flat fabrics.
Diluents: nitrogen.
Tested conditions: Oxygen 13.6 to 22.2%; Pressure 14.6959 psi; Pressure 101.325 kPa; Flow 0 to 55 cm/s.
Variables varied: ambient oxygen concentration, ventilation flow velocity, fuel type, fuel thickness, fuel geometry, oxygen concentration, flow velocity, sample geometry, sample width, rod diameter, flow speed, sample thickness, fuel material, airflow speed, thickness, geometry.
Tests recorded: 143.
Key findings: - The BASS-II experiments successfully utilized nitrogen dilution in the Microgravity Science Glovebox to study solid fuel combustion at reduced oxygen levels. - The global equivalence ratio for the tests was estimated to be fuel-rich, averaging 1.3, indicating under-ventilated combustion. - Heat release rates calculated from oxygen consumption were generally below 100 W for most of the tests. - The CO to CO2 ratios for these fires are an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases, indicating that these flames are not efficient. - For PMMA in ambient air, this transition thickness is evaluated to be 5.2 mm.
Ignition findings: - Astronauts observed unique transient phenomena during ignition and near extinction that were not visible from ground observations. - The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS. - At higher O2 concentrations, ignition occurred within approximately 40 s. Below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, the ignition delay time increased significantly. - Below an initial O2 concentration of ~14.5 percent O2, a sustained ignition could not be achieved even though flames were observed when the igniter was on and briefly after the igniter was turned off before extinguishing. - Ignition delay time increased significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached.
Flame spread findings: - At higher opposed-flow velocities, the flame spread rate is inversely proportional to fuel thickness and independent of the flow velocity, consistent with thermal theory. - In the microgravity regime, the flame spread rate decreases as the opposed-flow velocity is reduced, eventually leading to extinction. - the spread rate is independent of opposing flow velocity Vg for thin fuels while it is proportional to Vg for thick fuels. - the average flame spread rate increases with opposed-flow velocity, even within the small range of flow velocities tested. - Decreasing the rod diameter increases the flame spread rate in both 1g and microgravity environments
Extinction findings: - The critical flow velocity required to prevent radiative extinction is independent of the fuel thickness. - The critical extinction velocity increases significantly as the ambient oxygen concentration is reduced. - A simplified scale analysis was developed to predict the critical extinction velocity, showing good agreement with experimental and computational results. - At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed. - While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.
Fire safety relevance: Understanding flammability limits and flame growth rates in microgravity helps determine the worst-case fire scenarios in space, which is critical for developing safer spacecraft materials and effective firefighting strategies..

title: BASS structured summary
text:
Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS), NASA PSI investigation PSI-26.
Hardware: MSG.
Platform: ISS.
Years: 2009-2013.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in space. - Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
Fuel phase: solid.
Fuels: cotton-fiberglass blend, Nomex, Ultem, PMMA, wax, Japan wax, paraffin.
Sample geometry: flat sheets, solid spheres, and candles within tubes.
Diluents: nitrogen.
Tested conditions: Oxygen 21%; Flow 0 to 44 cm/s.
Variables varied: air flow speed, flow direction, sample width, fuel material, sample geometry.
Tests recorded: 133.
Key findings: - These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread). - Materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation may burn more readily compared to normal gravity with all other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.). - The custom-made cotton-fiberglass fabric performed very well, with none of the complications caused by the burnout of ordinary cellulosic fuel samples like paper. - This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity for a thin fuel with uniform burnout characteristics.
Flame spread findings: - For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed. - In the concurrent-flow configuration, flame size grew with time during the tests. A limiting length and steady spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds (<= 10 cm/s) for the short-length samples that fit in the small wind tunnel. - For concurrent flow, flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow. - Opposed-flow flame spread rate increases with flow to a maximum when the flow speed is around 10 to 15 cm/s and then decreases at higher speeds. - The concurrent-flow flame is longer and spreads twice as fast as the opposed-flow flame at 10 cm/s air flow speed.
Extinction findings: - By decreasing concurrent-flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s), quenching extinction was observed. - Based on the trends, it appears that an opposed-flow quenching extinction limit can be extrapolated to exist at an air flow speed of less than 1 cm/s. - The observation of the quenching extinction branch is only possible at microgravity, since otherwise any buoyant flow generated would take the system out of the low-speed flow regime.
Fire safety relevance: BASS results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. It helps bridge the gap between normal gravity material screening tests (like NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) and actual flammability in microgravity, where materials may burn more readily due to low-speed ventilation..

title: FLEX-2 structured summary
text:
Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2), NASA PSI investigation PSI-68.
Hardware: MDCA.
Platform: ISS.
Years: 2016-2019.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. - Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion. - Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries. - Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics. - Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays. - Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.
Fuel phase: liquid.
Fuels: n-heptane, methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol, n-octane, n-decane, n-butanol, gasoline, methyl butanoate, methyl decanoate, Jet-A, nonane, propanol, acetone, decane, hexanol, dodecane.
Sample geometry: droplet.
Diluents: helium, carbon dioxide, xenon, nitrogen.
Tested conditions: Oxygen 10 to 40%; Pressure 7.34795 to 44.0877 psi; Pressure 50.6625 to 303.975 kPa.
Variables varied: Fuel type, Ambient gas composition, Ambient Pressure, Droplet initial diameter, Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration), Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.
Tests recorded: 8.
Key findings: - Results indicate that ambient gas transport properties play an important role in determining flammability and combustion behaviors including burning rates and radiant heat output histories of the droplets. - Droplets would burn with significantly higher mole fractions of xenon than helium or carbon dioxide. - It is found that light diffraction at the droplet edge can contribute significantly to errors in droplet size measurements. - Other error sources include background light variations and partial coherence effects. - Results show that it is possible to automate data analysis for consecutive droplet burning images even in the presence of a significant amount of noise from soot formation. - An adaptive grayscale intensity threshold provides the ability to extract droplet diameters for the wide range of noise encountered. - In instances where soot blocks portions of the droplet, the algorithm manages to provide accurate measurements if a circle fit is used instead of an ellipse fit, as an ellipse can be too accommodating to the disturbance.
Ignition findings: - Comparison with previous experimental data shows that ignitability and combustion characteristics of droplets are influenced by the fuel type and also the gravitational level.
Flame spread findings: - Burning rates were about 40% to 70% higher in normal gravity than in reduced gravity. - Methanol droplets also had burning rates that were typically larger than 1-propanol burning rates by about 20% in reduced gravity. - In normal gravity, however, burning rate differences between the two fuels were significantly smaller. - After considering measurement uncertainties, burning rates decreased appreciably as the initial droplet diameter increased for combustion in air but not for combustion in the oxygen/helium environments. - It was also found that addition of either methanol or ethanol did not influence burning rates appreciably and that burning rates were larger for the oxygen/helium environments than for air if initial droplet diameter dependences were accounted for.
Extinction findings: - In reduced gravity, droplets would burn steadily with a xenon mole fraction of 0.50 but would not burn steadily if helium or carbon dioxide mole fractions were 0.50.
Fire safety relevance: Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies, future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency, and less pollutant emissions, as well as validation of jet engine models and development of fuel surrogates..

title: FLEX structured summary
text:
Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX), NASA PSI investigation PSI-69.
Hardware: CIR.
Platform: ISS.
Years: 2007-2016.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - Map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments - Measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6 - Develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions - Validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests - Obtain high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations
Fuel phase: liquid.
Fuels: methanol, n-heptane, n-octane, n-decane, n-butanol, gasoline, 1-propanol, methyl butanoate, methyl decanoate, Jet-A, camelina, tallow, nonane, acetone, ethanol.
Sample geometry: droplet.
Diluents: CO2, He, SF6, N2, xenon.
Tested conditions: Oxygen 12 to 34%; Pressure 7.348 to 44.859 psi; Pressure 50.6625 to 309.294 kPa.
Variables varied: ambient pressure, ambient oxygen mole fraction, droplet size, suppressant concentration, fuel type, diluent gas, gravity.
Tests recorded: 274.
Key findings: - Ambient gas transport properties play an important role in determining flammability and combustion behaviors including burning rates and radiant heat output histories of the droplets. - When a laminar diffusion flame is established over a spinning, thermoplastic, polymer fuel disc in a quiescent, oxidizing environment, the polymer melts and flows radially outwards, causing some fuel to be lost and not transported to the diffusion flame.
Flame spread findings: - After considering measurement uncertainties, burning rates decreased appreciably as the initial droplet diameter increased for combustion in air but not for combustion in the oxygen/helium environments. - Addition of either methanol or ethanol did not influence burning rates appreciably and burning rates were larger for the oxygen/helium environments than for air if initial droplet diameter dependences were accounted for. - Burning rates were about 40% to 70% higher in normal gravity than in reduced gravity. - Methanol droplets had burning rates that were typically larger than 1-propanol burning rates by about 20% in reduced gravity, whereas in normal gravity, burning rate differences between the two fuels were significantly smaller.
Extinction findings: - In reduced gravity, droplets would burn steadily with a xenon mole fraction of 0.50 but would not burn steadily if helium or carbon dioxide mole fractions were 0.50.
Fire safety relevance: By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft..

title: SAFFIRE-I structured summary
text:
Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I), NASA PSI investigation PSI-98.
Program: Saffire.
Hardware: other.
Platform: ISS.
Years: 2001-2008.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity - investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
Fuel phase: solid.
Fuels: SIBAL cloth, cotton, fiberglass.
Sample geometry: planar.
Tested conditions: Oxygen 21%; Flow 20 cm/s.
Variables varied: burn time.
Tests recorded: 4.
Fire safety relevance: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions..

title: SAME-R structured summary
text:
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (SAME-R), NASA PSI investigation PSI-101.
Hardware: MSG.
Platform: ISS.
Years: 2010-2014.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - Characterize the smoke aerosol encountered in space vehicles using the moment method in conjunction with the lognormal distribution assumption - Identify particle size distributions of aerosol produced from five tested materials commonly found in spacecraft - Examine the validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol particle size for the tested materials - make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors - Quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment - Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time (near the source) and smoke aging - Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison - Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test conditions - Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials
Fuel phase: solid.
Fuels: Teflon, Kapton, Pyrell, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), dibutyl-phthalate, cellulose, Silicone, Cellulose, DiButyl Phthalate.
Sample geometry: cylindrical.
Diluents: N2, nitrogen.
Tested conditions: Flow 0 to 8.1 cm/s.
Variables varied: material, heating temperature, air flow rate, aging time, sample temperature, air flow, weight loss rate, aging duration.
Tests recorded: 115.
Key findings: - Based on the results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles. - The comparatively much smaller diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices, on the other hand the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system. - It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests. - The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware. This resulted in a very high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume. - Silicone particles were not wholly preserved on the TEM grids owing to the volatile nature of the pyrolysis products. - Morphology results show that only Kapton and lamp wick are spherical aerosols so they are better suited to the moment method. - Overall the majority of the average smoke particle sizes were found to be in the 200 nm to 400 nm range with the quiescent cases producing some cases with substantially larger particles. - The aging results show a substantial increase in the observed diameters, with the increase in the count mean diameter being greater than the corresponding increase in the diameter of average mass. - Particle diameters for Teflon, Kapton, and lampwick show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow rates. - For all of the materials, the diameter of average mass is 30% to 40% larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests. - The zero-flow condition changed the morphology of Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres (at 8 cm/s flow) to spherical particles.
Fire safety relevance: The larger particle diameters observed in zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles..

title: SAME structured summary
text:
Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), NASA PSI investigation PSI-102.
Hardware: MSG.
Platform: ISS.
Years: 2000-2009.
Gravity: microgravity.
Objectives: - characterize the size distribution of smoke particulate produced in low-gravity from a variety of overheated spacecraft materials - obtain this data that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration missions - To make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors. - Quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. - Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the Μg smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time (near the source) and smoke aging. - Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison. - Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test conditions. - Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials
Fuel phase: solid.
Fuels: cellulose, Kapton, silicone rubber, Teflon, dibutyl-phthalate, Silicone Rubber, Cellulose, Dibutyl Phthalate.
Sample geometry: cylinder.
Diluents: nitrogen.
Tested conditions: Flow 5 to 10 cm/s.
Variables varied: airflow rates, pyrolysis temperatures, smoke aging durations, sample temperature, air flow rate, smoke aging duration, material, air flow, weight loss rate, aging duration.
Tests recorded: 16.
Key findings: - The experimental results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter. - The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. - The small diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices, on the other hand the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system, suggesting that detection of these particles against the background environment will require a detection system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution. - The aging results show substantial increase in the average particle sizes with them rising to over 1 Ιm for the aged silicone diameter of average mass. - The preliminary results from these experiments indicate that substantial differences in the size distributions of the smoke particles are evident for the four materials that were tested. - For the conditions of the SAME experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are better detected using an ionization smoke detector. - Smoke particulate produced in low-gravity was found to be typically 50% large in count mean diameter than similar conditions in normal gravity. - The resultant sizes were all below 300 nm suggesting that discriminating smoke from spacecraft dust possibly could be achieved by detecting in the sub-micrometer range. - Numerical modeling of smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the ISS predicted that actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on location and the presence of obstructions. - The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the smokes with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created in normal Earth gravity. - Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. - Overall the detection times were dominated by the circumferential flow, the axial flow from the intermodule ventilation and the smoke source strength.
Ignition findings: - In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, samples were heated to temperatures below the ignition point.
